title: Water Cycle Systems
subject: Science
developmentNotes: Students may memorize stage names without understanding energy, matter movement, and system interactions. Emphasize system flow and cause/effect.
learningObjective: Students will model the water cycle as a system, explain how water moves through reservoirs, and use evidence to describe the role of energy.
essentialQuestion: How does water move through Earth’s systems without disappearing?

vocabularyTerms.definition: liquid water changing into water vapor
water vapor cooling into liquid droplets
water falling from clouds as rain, snow, sleet, or hail
water gathering in oceans, lakes, rivers, soil, ice, or groundwater
a place where water is stored

prerequisites: Know states of matter: solid, liquid, gas

hook.content: Students imagine a single water droplet traveling from the ocean to a cloud, to a mountain, into a river, and back to the ocean. They predict what forces move it.
hook.studentAction: Predict, notice, or explain initial thinking before direct instruction.
hook.teacherOrAppAction: Capture initial response as non-graded diagnostic evidence.

miniTeach.content: The water cycle is a system powered mainly by the Sun and gravity. Water changes form and moves among reservoirs such as oceans, atmosphere, land, ice, living things, and groundwater. The amount of water is conserved; it changes location and form.
miniTeach.cognitiveLoadNotes: Use short chunks, one example at a time, and reveal labels only after students observe the model.

firstPrinciplesBreakdown.coreConcept: The water cycle is movement of water through a connected Earth system.
known: The Sun adds energy that can evaporate water.
Gravity pulls precipitation and runoff downhill.
Water can be stored in many reservoirs.
unknown: The path a specific water droplet will take next.
rules: Matter is conserved in the system.
avoid: Do not think water disappears when it evaporates.
Do not treat the cycle as always following one perfect circle.
Do not ignore groundwater, ice, plants, or storage.
steps: Name the energy or force involved.
firstPrinciplesBreakdown.check: If water seems to disappear, ask which form or reservoir it moved into.

workedExample.content: Ocean water gains energy from sunlight and evaporates into water vapor. The vapor rises and cools, condensing into cloud droplets. Droplets combine and fall as precipitation. Some water runs into rivers, some enters soil, and some returns to the ocean.
workedExample.teacherOrAppAction: Highlight each reasoning step and connect it to the first-principles breakdown.

items: Label processes on a water cycle diagram.
Explain which process requires heat energy.
Sort examples into reservoirs: atmosphere, ocean, groundwater, ice, living things.
Debug a diagram that skips collection and groundwater.
guidedPractice.scaffolding: Start with high support, then remove hints. Require explanation on the final item.

criticalThinkingCheckpoint.prompt: Why is “water cycle” a simplified model instead of an exact path every water molecule follows?
criticalThinkingCheckpoint.lookFor: Student identifies assumption, evaluates reasoning, and explains why one answer or model is stronger.

evidenceBasedReasoningTask.prompt: Claim: The Sun helps move water through the cycle. Use evaporation as evidence and explain the energy transfer.

interpretationOrDiscussionTask.prompt: Interpret arrows in a diagram: which arrows show energy-driven movement and which show gravity-driven movement?
interpretationOrDiscussionTask.safety: Use private response or moderated classroom mode only. No unrestricted student chat.

activePractice.content: Students simulate a water droplet journey by rolling process cards and building a path through reservoirs.

reteachPath.misconception: Student memorizes a simple circle and thinks water disappears or follows only one fixed path.
reteachPath.simpleExplanation: Water changes form and moves through connected places. The path can vary, but matter remains in the system.
steps: Label the process at each movement.
Name the energy or force involved.
Add an overlooked reservoir like groundwater.

practice.answer: It becomes vapor in the atmosphere.

reteachPath.exitCriteria: Student completes at least 4 of 5 reteach items and explains the corrected misconception.

tasks: Create two different water droplet journeys and compare them.

Explain how drought affects reservoirs and movement.

successCriteria: I can trace water through more than one reservoir.
I can name the process and energy or condition that drives a change.
I can use a model to explain why water does not disappear.
I can predict how a changed condition could affect the system.

knowledge: Water changes form and moves among connected reservoirs.
Energy and conditions drive processes such as evaporation and condensation.
capability: Use evidence to explain a water movement.
reasoning: Distinguish naming a process from explaining its cause and effect.
retention: Retrieve the water-cycle process sequence and system idea after a delay.
transfer: Apply the model to drought, pavement, forests, or temperature changes.

phaseModules.title: Follow one water droplet
phaseModules.studentAction: Predict where a droplet could travel and what might make it change form.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can state a testable starting idea.

phaseModules.title: See matter and energy move
phaseModules.studentAction: Watch a labeled model connect reservoirs, processes, arrows, and the Sun's energy.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can point to where water is stored and how it moves.

phaseModules.title: Separate stage names from explanations
phaseModules.studentAction: Sort observations, process names, energy sources, and cause-and-effect explanations.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can explain what causes one process instead of only naming it.

phaseModules.title: Build the system map
phaseModules.studentAction: Place reservoir and process cards in more than one valid droplet path and label the arrows.
phaseModules.successCheck: My model shows connected movement, not a fixed circle only.

phaseModules.title: Explain a changed condition
phaseModules.studentAction: Use evidence to predict how heat, wind, pavement, drought, or forest loss could change movement.
phaseModules.successCheck: I connect a condition to a process and a reservoir.

phaseModules.title: Complete the systems checkpoint
phaseModules.studentAction: Answer the water-cycle questions and explain one arrow in the model independently.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can support the explanation with the model.

phaseModules.title: Retrieve the droplet story
phaseModules.studentAction: Return later and reconstruct a droplet path without looking at the original diagram.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can retrieve process, reservoir, and driver relationships.

phaseModules.title: Investigate a local change
phaseModules.studentAction: Apply the model to a changed surface, weather pattern, or plant environment.
phaseModules.successCheck: The system model works in a new context.

phaseModules.title: Choose reteach or challenge
phaseModules.studentAction: Repair missing arrows or causes, or extend the model with a human impact and testable prediction.
phaseModules.successCheck: My next move matches the model evidence.

feedbackRules.result: The learner treats evaporation as water being destroyed.

feedbackRules.result: The learner thinks every droplet follows one identical route.

reteachPaths.trigger: The learner lists process names without causes.

challengePaths.trigger: The learner explains connected water-cycle processes.
challengePaths.action: Predict how pavement, forest loss, drought, or a temperature shift changes runoff, evaporation, and storage.

parentTeacherNotes: On a rainy or hot day, ask the student where water is moving and which process is happening.
accessibilityNotes: Use plain, grade-appropriate language and define academic vocabulary before using it in prompts.
Provide alt text or text-equivalent descriptions for every image, diagram, array, chart, map, or model.
Make all interactive elements keyboard accessible with visible focus states and screen-reader labels.
Never rely only on color to communicate correct/incorrect, categories, or importance.
Provide read-aloud support for Foundation Academy and optional read-aloud for all grade bands.
Chunk instructions into short steps and provide examples before independent work.
safetyNotes: No public student posting, random direct messages, or unrestricted discussion.
Discussion prompts must use sentence frames and moderation/teacher controls when implemented.
Student-generated work should be visible only to the student and authorized parent/teacher roles unless explicitly assigned in a safe classroom workflow.
Do not collect unnecessary personal information in lesson responses.
implementationNotes: Render lessonFlow sections in order with progress state.
Persist quiz attempts and item-level skill tags.
Generate Memory Vault records after lesson completion.
Use mastery bands to branch to reteach, guided practice, review, or challenge.
Store open responses privately with role-based access.
Use answer keys and rubrics for review; do not expose hidden answer keys in student mode.
